title: India’s village budgets depend on transfers, while service quality depends on what happens after construction
summary: Roughly nine-tenths of the receipts of the Indian village councils studied by the Reserve Bank came from intergovernmental transfers. This makes the size and timing of grants central to rural public spending. It also limits what a larger grant allocation alone can deliver. The RBI’s second biennial report finds that greater funding was associated with greater spending on core services, while access, quality and the continued functioning of assets varied considerably across states and villages. The distinction matters for judging whether a fiscal commitment will generate near-term orders for suppliers and whether the resulting infrastructure will continue to provide services.

The RBI constructed a balanced panel of 225,458 Gram Panchayats covering fiscal years 2022–23 to 2024–25. It required non-zero receipts and expenditure in all three years, removed observations in the top and bottom 0.5% of the distributions and matched the receipt and expenditure records. Table II.1 covers the participating states. The overview describes the panel as about 85% of all Gram Panchayats. The largely provisional 2024–25 figures and the exclusion of councils with missing reports matter when comparing states. A common sample makes year-to-year changes easier to interpret, but poorly recorded or very small councils may operate with different constraints (chapter II, section 2).

Own-source revenue supplied about one-tenth of total receipts and came predominantly from non-tax sources. States differed in the powers, property records, staff and collection systems available to councils. A weak own-revenue share can reflect limited legal authority or a weak local base as well as collection performance. Moreover, tied grants impose conditions on where funds can be spent. Water and sanitation accounted for about 40% of expenditure, reflecting Finance Commission mandates and alignment with national programmes. This concentration is relevant to investors or contractors estimating the mix of rural spending. It gives little basis for simply applying nationwide growth in grants to every market for local infrastructure (chapter II, charts II.5 and II.12–16).

The report connects expenditure to physical, digital and social infrastructure across states. Rural roads, electricity, water and sanitation networks have expanded, but a recorded asset or connection need not mean reliable service. The ability to coordinate with other government tiers, provide staff and pay for operation and maintenance matters after construction. Broad regional comparisons are descriptive. Areas able to record spending consistently and implement projects effectively may also differ in income, institutions or the availability of national programme funding. The report therefore supports inspecting functionality as well as construction outlays before inferring wider local economic gains (chapter III and its state annexures).

Future grants could increase room for local decisions. The Sixteenth Finance Commission recommended ₹4.35 lakh crore in rural local-body grants for 2026–31, 83.8% above the Fifteenth Commission recommendation. Of the new grant total, 80% is a basic component and 20% is performance based. Half of the performance component becomes linked to improvements in own-source revenue from the third year. Half of the basic component is tied, while the previous commission tied 60% of total grants. The denominators differ. These recommendations are a multiyear envelope, separate from the actual receipts in the historical panel and from the annual cash releases any particular state or council will receive. The RBI emphasises timely transfers, better local planning and maintenance, and stronger local revenue institutions (chapter IV).

questions.question: When will recommended grants become spendable cash for village councils?
questions.detail: The report distinguishes allocations from transfers and stresses predictability. Reconcile commission recommendations with state budgets, release orders and actual receipts in local accounting records, separating basic and performance components. The timing matters for the cash flow of contractors and suppliers and for the fiscal impulse in any one quarter. A larger multiyear envelope can accompany uneven near-term execution.

questions.question: Which local spending produces services that remain functional?
questions.detail: Compare spending by function with project completion, connection reliability, maintenance expenditure and access at the village level. Chapter III’s administrative indicators and state annexures are starting points. Account for overlapping national schemes and differences in local implementation capacity. A region with high capital outlays but poor maintenance could generate construction demand without the same long-term improvement in productive capacity.

questions.question: Where can own-source revenue respond to a performance incentive?
questions.detail: Compare councils’ legal authority, taxable property registers, user charges, collection costs and household ability to pay before interpreting changes in the ratio. Test whether an apparent improvement reflects higher recurring receipts, reclassification or a temporary decline in transfers. The answer would help distinguish stronger fiscal autonomy from a change in the recorded funding mix and assess which councils might qualify for future performance grants.
